In mathematics, the '''Jacquet–Langlands correspondence''' is a correspondence  between [[automorphic form]]s on [[General linear group|GL<sub>2</sub>]] and its twisted forms, proved by {{Harvs|txt|author1-link=Hervé Jacquet|last=Jacquet|author2-link=Robert Langlands|last2=Langlands|year=1970|loc=section 16}} in their book ''[[Automorphic Forms on GL(2)]]'' using the [[Selberg trace formula]]. It was one of the first examples of the [[Langlands philosophy]] that maps between [[Langlands dual|L-group]]s should induce maps between [[automorphic representations]]. There are generalized versions of the Jacquet–Langlands correspondence relating automorphic representations of GL<sub>''r''</sub>(''D'') and GL<sub>''dr''</sub>(''F''), where ''D'' is a [[division algebra]] of degree ''d''<sup>2</sup> over the [[Local field|local]] or [[global field]] ''F''.

Suppose that ''G''  is an inner twist of the algebraic group GL<sub>2</sub>, in other words the [[multiplicative group]] of a [[quaternion algebra]]. The Jacquet–Langlands correspondence is [[bijection]] between
*[[Automorphic representation]]s of ''G''  of dimension greater than 1
*Cuspidal automorphic  representations of GL<sub>2</sub> that are [[Square-integrable function|square integrable]] (modulo the center) at each [[Ramification (mathematics)|ramified]] place of ''G''.
Corresponding representations have the same local components at all unramified places of ''G''.

{{harvtxt|Rogawski|1983}} and {{harvtxt|Deligne|Kazhdan|Vignéras|1984}} extended the Jacquet–Langlands correspondence to division algebras of higher dimension.
